Juho Kusti Paasikivi (27 November 1870 – 14 December 1956) was a Finnish politician who served as the president of Finland from 1946 to 1956. Representing the Finnish Party until its dissolution in 1918 and then the National Coalition Party, he previously served as senator, member of parliament (1907–1909, 1910–1914), envoy to Stockholm (1936–1939) and Moscow (1940–1941), and Prime Minister of Finland (1918 and 1944–1946).

Every biography of Juho Kusti Paasikivi has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. He also held several other positions of trust, and was an influential figure in Finnish economics and politics for over fifty years. Paasikivi was also the last Finnish president born in the 1800s and the "lowest" in terms of social origin.

The education of Juho Kusti Paasikivi happened mostly outside any school. Hellsten's parents lived in Tampere, but the son was born on their business trip to the Lahti market. Hellsten's mother died when he was four, and his father died in debt when Hellsten was 14.

What Juho Kusti Paasikivi wanted at the start and what Juho Kusti Paasikivi got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Upon his father's death, Hellsten's aunt, Kaisa Hagman, assumed responsibility for his raising. His father had recognized his son's academic talent and enrolled him at a top elementary school in Hämeenlinna following brief attendance at Hollola.

The defining trait of Juho Kusti Paasikivi was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. Paasikivi exhibited an early appetite for reading, and was the best pupil in his class. He entered the University of Helsinki in 1890, graduating in May 1892 with a Bachelor's degree in Russian language and literature, a course of studies that proved useful in later life.

Those who met Juho Kusti Paasikivi at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. He also studied law at the universities of Leipzig, Stockholm and Uppsala, receiving his Doctor of Law in 1902. During his schooling, Paasikivi supported himself by working variously as a teacher, lecturer, court bailiff, and lawyer in private practice in Lahti.

The private years of Juho Kusti Paasikivi explain the public decades better than any speech. It was also during his university studies, around 1894, that Paasikivi first became involved in the Fennoman movement, assuming leadership roles in its student organization. Together they had four children, Annikki (1898–1950), Wellamo (1900–1966), Juhani (1901–1942), and Varma (1903–1941).

The family Juho Kusti Paasikivi came from matters more than the legends admit. Upon earning his doctorate in law in 1901, Paasikivi took on an associate professorship of Administrative Law at Helsinki University from 1902 to 1903. Paasikivi left this post to become Director-in-Chief of Treasury of the Grand Duchy of Finland, a position he retained until 1914.

The first real success of Juho Kusti Paasikivi arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. For practically all of his adult life, Paasikivi moved in the inner circles of Finland's politics. He supported greater autonomy and an independent Cabinet (Senate) for Finland, and resisted Russia's panslavic intentions to make Russian the only official language everywhere in the Russian Empire.

The last chapter of Juho Kusti Paasikivi was written long after the fame. He belonged, however, to the more complying Finnish Party, opposing radical and potentially counter-productive steps which could be perceived as aggressive by the Russians. Paasikivi served as a Finnish Party member of Parliament 1907–1909 and 1910–1913.

The whole life of Juho Kusti Paasikivi reads like a single decision repeated. During the First World War Paasikivi began to doubt the Finnish Party's obedient line. In 1914, after resigning his position at the Treasury, and also standing down as a member of Parliament, Paasikivi left public life and office.

Between the birth and the legend of Juho Kusti Paasikivi lie the years that actually decide it. Paasikivi also served as a member of the City Council of Helsinki 1915–1918. After the 1917 February Revolution in Russia, Paasikivi was appointed to the committee that began formulating new legislation for a modernized Grand Duchy.

The reputation of Juho Kusti Paasikivi was built in the middle, not at the edges. Initially he supported increased autonomy within the Russian state, in opposition to the Social Democrats in the coalition-Senate, who in vain strove for more far-reaching autonomy; but after the 1917 Bolshevik October Revolution, Paasikivi championed full independence—in the form of constitutional monarchy. During the Civil War in Finland Paasikivi stood firmly on the side of the White government.

Somebody like Juho Kusti Paasikivi should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. As prime minister from May until November 1918, he strove for a continued constitutional monarchy with Frederick Charles of Hesse, a German Prince, as king, intending to ensure German support for Finland against Bolshevist Russia. However, as Germany lost the World War, the monarchy had to be scrapped for a republic more in the taste of the victorious Entente.

The life of Juho Kusti Paasikivi begins far from where the story usually starts. Paasikivi's Senate was in power during the existence of the prison camps following the Civil War in Finland, where 12,000 prisoners died in total. Starvation was seen as a principal cause of mortality in the camps which housed men and women who had fought on the side of the Reds.

Juho Kusti Paasikivi was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Paasikivi, as a political conservative, was a firm opponent of Social Democrats in the cabinet, or communists in the Parliament. Tentatively he supported the semi-fascist Lapua movement, which requested radical measures against the political Left.

To understand where Juho Kusti Paasikivi ended up, start with where Juho Kusti Paasikivi began. But eventually the Lapua movement radicalized further, even assaulting Ståhlberg, liberal former president of Finland; and Paasikivi like many other supporters, turned away from the radical right. In 1934 he became chairman of the conservative National Coalition Party, as a champion of democracy, and successfully rehabilitated the party after its suspicious closeness to the Lapua movement and the failed coup d'état, the Mäntsälä Rebellion.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Juho Kusti Paasikivi ran through years nobody filmed. Widowed in 1931, he married Allina (Alli) Valve (1879–1960) in 1934 and resigned from politics. However, he was persuaded to accept the position of Envoy to Sweden, at the time regarded as Finland's most important foreign embassy post.

Each stage of the life of Juho Kusti Paasikivi made the next stage possible. The threats from totalitarian regimes that had seized power in Germany and the Soviet Union made Finland increasingly isolated. With the gradual weakening of the League of Nations, and France's and the United Kingdom's apparent lack of interest in supporting Finland, Sweden was the only notable power left that could possibly provide Finland any support at all.

The people who knew Juho Kusti Paasikivi young describe someone already restless. Since around the time of the failed Lapua coup, Paasikivi and Mannerheim had belonged to a close circle of conservative Finns discussing how Sweden's support could be obtained. In Stockholm Paasikivi strove for Swedish defence guarantees, alternatively a defensive alliance or a defensive union between Finland and Sweden.

What Juho Kusti Paasikivi built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Since the Civil War, relations between the Swedes and Finns had been frosty. The revolutionary turmoil at the end of World War I had led to Parliamentarism in Sweden, increased Swedish democracy, and a dominant role for the Swedish Social Democrats.

By the time Juho Kusti Paasikivi reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. In Finland, however, the result had been a disastrous Civil War and a total defeat for Socialism. At the same time that Paasikivi arrived in Stockholm, it became known that Finnish President Svinhufvud retained his aversion to parliamentarism; and (after pressure from Paasikivi's National Coalition Party) had declined to appoint a cabinet with Social Democrats as Ministers.

The rise of Juho Kusti Paasikivi was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. This didn't improve Paasikivi's reputation among the Swedish Social Democrats dominating the government, who were sufficiently suspicious due to his association with Finland's Monarchist orientation in 1918, and the failed Lapua coup in 1932. Things actually improved, partly due to Paasikivi's efforts, partly due to President Kallio being elected.

Setbacks came early for Juho Kusti Paasikivi, and the response to them is the real story. As president, Kallio approved of parliamentarism and appointed Social Democrats to the cabinet. But the suspicions between Finland and Sweden were too strong: During the Winter War Sweden's support for Finland was considerable, but short of one critical feature: Sweden neither declared war on the Soviet Union nor sent regular troops to Finland's defense.

The legacy of Juho Kusti Paasikivi outlived the circumstances that produced it. This made many Finns, including Paasikivi himself, judge his mission in Stockholm a failure. Prior to the Winter War, Paasikivi became the Finnish representative in the negotiations in Moscow.

Few lives travel as far as that of Juho Kusti Paasikivi, and the distance is the point. Seeing that Joseph Stalin did not intend to change his policies, Paasikivi supported compliance with some of the demands. When the war broke out, Paasikivi was asked to enter Risto Ryti’s cabinet as a minister without portfolio—in practice in the role of a distinguished political advisor.

The childhood of Juho Kusti Paasikivi contains the adult in small print. He ended up in the cabinet's leading triumvirate together with Risto Ryti and Foreign Minister Väinö Tanner (chairman of the Social Democrats). Paasikivi also led the negotiations for an armistice and peace, and continued his mission in Moscow as Envoy.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Juho Kusti Paasikivi — in that order. In Moscow he was necessarily isolated from the most secret thoughts in Helsinki; and when he found out that these thoughts ran in the direction of revanche, of retaking, with Germany's aid, territory lost in the Winter War, he resigned. In summer 1941, when the Continuation War began, Paasikivi took up writing his memoirs.

The turning point in the life of Juho Kusti Paasikivi looked like a failure at the time. By 1943 he had concluded that Germany was going to lose the war and that Finland was in great danger as well. However, his initial opposition to the pro-German politics of 1940–1941 was too well known, and his first initiatives for peace negotiations were met with little support from either Field Marshal Mannerheim or Risto Ryti, who now had become President.

Every biography of Juho Kusti Paasikivi has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. For the first time in Finland a Communist, Yrjö Leino, was included in the cabinet. Paasikivi's policies were to be "realistic", radically different from those of the previous 25 years.

The education of Juho Kusti Paasikivi happened mostly outside any school. Paasikivi sought to understand why Moscow had ordered the invasion of Finland in 1939. He concluded  that interwar Finnish portrayals of the Soviet Union were "heedlessly Russophobic", and that the Soviet attack was legitimate, strategic, and  even "defensive" rather than ideological or expansionist.

What Juho Kusti Paasikivi wanted at the start and what Juho Kusti Paasikivi got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Consequently, he ensured that negative references to the Soviet Union were expunged from school textbooks and that books containing "hostile" representations of the Soviet Union were removed from public libraries. Paasikivi had to comply with many Soviet demands, including the war crimes trial.

The defining trait of Juho Kusti Paasikivi was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. His main effort was to prove that Finland would present no threat to the Soviet Union, and that both countries would gain from confident peaceful relations. When Mannerheim resigned, Parliament selected Paasikivi to succeed him as President of the Republic; Paasikivi was then aged 75.
